extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and computer scientists writing research papers, expositions, and textbooks
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing mathematical and computer-science papers, lecture notes, and textbooks, covering exposition, proofs, organization, examples, and publication choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get attention immediately
rubrics_metrics.description: Get the attention of your readers immediately. Use snappy titles, arresting first sentences, and lucid initial paragraphs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited: Gleason's memorable title, Thurston's opening question, and Taussky-Todd's autobiographical first paragraph. A notable author reputation helps but craft the opening to 'leap out' at readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell readers up front what you're doing
rubrics_metrics.description: Get everything up front. Tell your readers in plain English what you are going to write about and let them decide whether they are interested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarize goals and results early — 'you can quintuple your readership' by being explicit about the paper's content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make results easy to find for skimmers
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers scan papers; potential readers will skim looking for statements of theorems and key results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarize results using boldface (or other emphasis) so skimmers can find them; avoid long discursive text where readers expect theorems or statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid heavy notation in theorem statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Drop notational abbreviations and convoluted references in the statements of theorems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make theorem statements readable and self-contained; don't force readers to parse dense notation in the main claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give modest motivation; don't overdo examples
rubrics_metrics.description: A little motivation is good, but readers don't like too much; presenting examples that fail to yield results can be useful but loses charm if overused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a few well-chosen motivating examples; avoid many gratuitous examples or mysterious 'Consider the following ...' setups that signal weak motivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance chatty exposition with lean proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a mixed style: be chatty and expository leading up to proofs and after them, but be 'lean and mean' in the proofs themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use conversational, explanatory prose for intuition and context, then present concise rigorous proofs, and return to exposition afterward as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use short, self-contained problems/exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems that are self-contained and digestible help readers build understanding of bigger results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Polya & Szego's Problems and Theorems of Analysis — problems with spare answers encourage deep thinking; include exercises that guide readers toward larger theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use many examples in textbooks
rubrics_metrics.description: Textbooks should contain lots of examples; even simple examples convey large parts of an idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide simple examples to get three-quarters of an idea across, then refine with more elaborate examples later. Finding the right examples is time-consuming but crucial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Put yourself in the reader's place
rubrics_metrics.description: Always consider the reader's perspective when writing and organizing exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate readers' difficulties and confusions; write to the primitives the reader has and keep cognitive load manageable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read about a topic before writing it up
rubrics_metrics.description: Spend time reading about a topic and then write in the evening to obtain the right expository order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practice helps order material naturally and preserves the perspective of a learner, which aids exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep definitions close to their uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't separate definitions from where they are used; readers don't like having to flip chapters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeat definitions if necessary; it's better to be slightly redundant than to force readers to hunt for definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep exposition accessible; avoid opaque machinery
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using powerful technical machinery if it makes exposition too opaque; prefer basic calculations and accessibility where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to teach underlying mechanics (e.g., 20 pages of asymptotics) or to state results with references; keep exposition at a level readers can follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: State variable types and concrete notation
rubrics_metrics.description: State the types of your variables explicitly (e.g., 'the set S' not just 'S').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear typing and notation prevent ambiguity; encourage explicitness in variable declarations to help readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid non-referential uses of 'this'
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using the non-referential 'this', which often confuses readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many texts forbid such usages; ambiguous 'this' sentences can leave readers bewildered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use analogy selectively
rubrics_metrics.description: Use analogy, metaphor, and simile where they clearly illuminate and the reader will 'get the point.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy can be effective (as in physics texts) but should be used only when it aids understanding rather than introducing confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborate to filter idiosyncrasies
rubrics_metrics.description: Find co-authors to help filter out personal idiosyncrasies and improve quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Co-authors may not save time but help produce a more balanced text; small improvements can yield large market advantages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use many small, well-chosen examples in exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Even a very simple example will get most of an idea across; follow-up with complex examples that show subtleties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spend time finding examples that illustrate 'all and only' the points you intend; good examples are hard to find but high-impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit and cautious about quotations and plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: When quoting, be explicit; avoid verbatim copying and suspicious similarities in notation or typography.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plagiarism can be detected by identical phrasing, equations, or even italic usage; attribution and explicit quoting remove doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose an appropriate publication venue
rubrics_metrics.description: Select venue according to polish and permanence: journals for polished, timeless work; conferences for rougher, not-yet-archival work; tech reports for very preliminary material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always remember that there are readers for each format; a tech report may later become a journal paper, so maintain clarity and care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't write for the wrong motivations
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid writing papers merely to boost publication lists or to get into a specific proceedings; write because you are excited about your results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poor motivations often produce sloppy papers and post-publication corrections; judge whether a work is worth publishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware conceits and themes
rubrics_metrics.description: A conceit or thematic framing can catalyze writing but should not intrude or be forced; be willing to abandon cute themes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance creativity with clarity; jokes and dated conceits can age badly and distract from the ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid early focus on formatting; think structure first
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't fret formatting while drafting; prioritize logical structure and use macros for complex notation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use structural tools (macros) to manage complex notation and keep focus on content organization rather than typesetting early on.

rubrics_metrics.name: First sentence must be strong and direct
rubrics_metrics.description: Craft a strong, nontechnical, direct first sentence that avoids passive constructions and grabs attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good first sentence sets reader expectations; subsequent sentences must maintain the same energy and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use structured proofs (statement-reason/tabular) to clarify logic
rubrics_metrics.description: Write proofs in a 'statement - reason' tabular form to enforce structure and clarify arguments, then convert to paragraphs if desired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The tabular form can reveal redundant or bloated prose and help trim and clarify paragraph proofs; example provided from Spivak's calculus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition: organize and simplify
rubrics_metrics.description: Composition is the combination of organisation and simplification; writing should be composed with these aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply photographic sense of composition: present the strongest view by organizing and simplifying material for reader construction and participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start early and make writing a habit
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin writing early; frequent practice (essays, short pieces) develops clear organization and style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Starting early lets writing become a compulsion in a productive way; teaching material while writing helps ensure correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewrite repeatedly and solicit critiques
rubrics_metrics.description: Expect to rewrite many times; seek critiques from others before publishing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most works need many revisions; peer feedback (colleagues, students) helps catch oversights and improves clarity; new editions are opportunities to correct errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read widely to learn writing craft
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn to write by reading great literature and exemplary technical exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exposure to strong authors (both within and outside the field) sharpens style and critical faculties; emulate good models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model the reader; build internal error-checkers
rubrics_metrics.description: Operationalize 'model the reader' with internal 'deemons' that catch likely misunderstandings and stylistic errors automatically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train habits to flag split infinitives, ambiguous references, and other common pitfalls; the checks should become automatic rather than conscious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master the medium: typography, figures, indexes
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn and use the tools of the medium (vocabulary, indexes, tables, graphs, typography) to present material effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typography can mark logical distinctions (e.g., typewriter font for formulas); invest attention in effective use of tables, graphs, and indexing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master the material by teaching and organizing
rubrics_metrics.description: Mastery of the subject matter is essential; writing organizes thought and deepens understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teaching the material while writing (e.g., running a course) provides internal feedback and reveals gaps; writing should reflect a strong internal model of the material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make writing enjoyable
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing should be fun and joyful; authors should feel pleasure in the act of composing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate a personal environment and tools that make writing pleasurable — this sustains long-term effort and creativity.
